title: Count Distinct Island Shapes
statement:
You get an m × n grid of 0 (water) and 1 (land). An island is a group of land cells joined up, down, left or right.

Two islands have the same shape if one can be slid onto the other exactly, without rotating or mirroring it. Return the number of different shapes among all the islands.

examples.why: Three islands: two horizontal pairs and one single cell. The two pairs share a shape, so there are 2 shapes.
An L and a straight bar, both three cells. Grouping islands by size would wrongly report 1.
Both islands are L shapes of three cells, but one is a rotation of the other. Rotations count as different shapes.

hints: Finding the islands is a standard flood fill. The new part is deciding when two islands are the same shape.
Slide each island so that its first cell (the first one met in row-major order) sits at (0, 0). Two islands match exactly when their shifted cell sets match.
Turn each shifted cell list into a string such as "0,0;0,1;1,1" and add it to a set. The answer is the size of the set.

explain.intuition:
Finding islands is plain DFS over a grid. To compare shapes, describe every island in coordinates relative to a fixed anchor. If you scan the grid row by row, the first cell you touch in each island is its top-most, then left-most cell. Subtract that anchor from every cell of the island and you get a description that does not depend on where the island sits.

Two islands are translations of each other exactly when their relative cell sets are equal. Collect the cells in a fixed order (for example, sort them, or record them in the same DFS visiting order), join them into a string and put the string in a set. Rotations and mirror images give different strings, which is what the rules ask for. It is like normalising a set of absolutely positioned elements to the top-left of their bounding box before comparing layouts.
steps: Scan the grid. When you find an unvisited land cell (r0, c0), start a DFS from it.
During the DFS mark cells visited and record (r − r0, c − c0) for each one.
Sort the recorded offsets and join them into a key string.
Add the key to a set, and return the set's size at the end.
pitfalls: Comparing islands by size only. Different shapes can have the same number of cells.
Storing absolute coordinates, so equal shapes in different places look different.
Recording only the DFS direction letters without a marker for when the DFS backs up. Two different shapes can then produce the same string. Sorting relative offsets avoids that.

complexity.time: O(m · n · log(m · n)) with sorting

solutions.title: Relative offsets, sorted, in a set
solutions.idea: Flood fill each island, shift it so its first cell is the origin, sort the offsets and use them as a key.

solutions.title: DFS path signature with backtrack markers
solutions.idea: Record the direction of every DFS step and a marker each time the DFS returns. With a fixed neighbour order, equal shapes produce equal strings and no sort is needed.

followups: Rotations and mirror images now count as the same shape. How do you build a canonical key for all 8 orientations?
The grid streams in one row at a time and is too big to hold. Can you still count shapes?
